Signs:
• Red skin
• Pain
• No blisters

Treatment:
• Cool water 10–20 minutes
• Aloe vera or mild moisturizer after cooling
• Pain reliever (like paracetamol or ibuprofen)
• Usually heals in 3–7 days

Signs:
• Blisters
• Swelling
• Very painful
• Wet or shiny skin

Treatment:
• Cool water immediately (very important)
• Do NOT pop blisters
• Cover with sterile non-stick dressing
• Pain relief meds
• Keep clean and dry
• May take 1–3 weeks to heal

See a doctor if:
• Burn is larger than your palm
• On face, hands, feet, or genitals
• Signs of infection (pus, fever, bad smell)

Example:
Fire, electric shock, chemical burn

Signs:
• White, black, or charred skin
• May not hurt (nerves destroyed)
• Very deep damage

Treatment:
• Call emergency help or go to hospital immediately
• Do NOT remove stuck clothing
• Cover loosely with clean cloth
• Do NOT apply water for long periods if extensive burn (just protect and get help)

Usually the mildest type.

What it looks like:
• Blood oozes slowly
• Bright red or dark red
• Comes from scrapes or small cuts

Common scenarios:
• Knee scrape from falling
• Small kitchen knife cut
• Paper cut

Treatment:
• Wash hands if possible
• Clean wound with clean water
• Apply gentle pressure using clean cloth or gauze
• Put antiseptic if available
• Cover with bandage

Usually stops within minutes.

Watch for:
• Dirt inside wound

Infection signs:
• swelling
• pus
• redness spreading
• fever

Comes from veins. More serious than capillary bleeding.

What it looks like:
• Steady flow of dark red blood
• Does NOT usually spurt
• Can bleed heavily

Common scenarios:
• Deep cut from glass
• Knife injury
• Accident involving sharp metal

Treatment:
• Apply firm direct pressure immediately
• Raise injured area above heart if possible
• Use clean cloth/gauze
• Keep pressure for at least 10 minutes
• Add more cloth if blood soaks through
• Do NOT remove the first cloth

When to get help:
• Bleeding won’t stop
• Large wound
• Person becomes pale, weak, dizzy

Most dangerous type.

What it looks like:
• Bright red blood
• Spurts or pulses with heartbeat
• Heavy and fast bleeding

Common scenarios:
• Serious accident
• Deep stab wound
• Machinery injury
• Major trauma

Treatment:
• Call emergency help immediately
• Apply VERY firm pressure
• Use both hands if needed
• If possible, elevate the limb
• If bleeding is life-threatening and won’t stop: use a tourniquet above the wound
• Note the time applied

Important:
A person can lose dangerous amounts of blood very fast.

Watch for shock:
• cold skin
• confusion
• weakness
• rapid breathing
• fainting

Lay them down and keep them warm while waiting for help.
Illustration for choking above 1 year old

1. Encourage coughing
If they can cough hard, let them try first.

• Stand slightly behind them.
• Lean them forward.
• Give 5 strong back blows between the shoulder blades using your palm.

• Stand behind them.
• Wrap your arms around their waist.
• Make a fist, place it just above the belly button.
• Grab fist with your other hand.
• Pull inward and upward quickly.
• Do 5 thrusts.

Repeat:
5 back blows + 5 abdominal thrusts until object comes out or they collapse.

• Hold baby face-down on your forearm.
• Support head and jaw (keep head lower than body).
• Give 5 firm back blows between shoulder blades.

• Turn baby face-up on your arm.
• Use 2 fingers in the center of the chest (just below nipple line).
• Give 5 quick chest thrusts.

Repeat:
5 back blows + 5 chest thrusts until object comes out.
Laying the person on their back illustration
Gently lay the person on their back on a safe, not crowded area.

1. Check breathing

Look for:
• pulse
• chest movement
• normal breathing sounds

Place:
• heel of one hand on the center of the chest
• second hand on top

The correct spot:
• middle of chest
• lower half of breastbone

Interlock fingers.

Keep fingers off the ribs.

Body position
• Keep your arms straight
• Shoulders directly above hands

Use body weight, not just arm strength.

Chest compressions

Push:
• hard
• fast

Compression depth:
about 2 inches (5 cm)

Rate:
100–120 compressions per minute

Allow full chest recoil after every push.

Do not lean on the chest.

Give 30 compressions.

OPENING THE AIRWAY

Head tilt–chin lift
• Place one hand on forehead
• Tilt head back gently
• Lift chin with two fingers

This opens the airway.

How to give breaths
• Pinch nose closed
• Seal your mouth over theirs
• Give 1 breath for about 1 second

Watch for chest rise.

Give:
2 breaths total

If chest does not rise:
• reposition head
• try again

STEP 7: CONTINUE CPR

Repeat:
• 30 compressions
• 2 breaths

Continue until:
• help arrives
• AED is ready
• person breathes normally
• you are too exhausted

WHAT NOT TO DO
• Don’t try to push bone back
• Don’t force movement
• Don’t give food/drink if surgery might be needed
• Don’t ignore pain even if it seems minor

1. Keep the person still
• Do not move the injured part
• Movement can make it worse

2. Control bleeding (if any)
• Use clean cloth or bandage
• Apply gentle pressure
• If bone is sticking out, do NOT push it back

• Use a splint (wood, stick, cardboard, etc.)
• Secure with cloth, bandage, or tape
• Keep it in the position you found it

• Wrap ice in cloth
• Apply 10–15 minutes
• Helps reduce swelling

5. Elevate (if possible)
• Only if it doesn’t cause more pain
Helping a person lie down after fainting illustration
Raising the legs after fainting illustration
Staying with and reassuring a person who fainted illustration

• Lay them flat on their back
• This improves blood flow to the brain

If they can’t lie down:
• sit them down
• lower their head between their knees

• Lift legs about 12 inches (30 cm)
• Use a bag, chair, or pillow

This helps blood return to the brain.

• Loosen collar, belt, or tight clothes
• Helps breathing and circulation

• Most people wake up in 1–2 minutes
• Keep them calm

Do NOT let them stand up right away.
